title: One competitor outside the company, one inside it
lede: New Coke was built to beat Pepsi. The drink that beat it was the one it had replaced.

blocks.title: Four colas, one casualty
blocks.subtitle: What each was, and what became of it.

items.name: New Coke / Coke II
items.text: Share in its first year and in 1999, by one later account.[^16] Withdrawn in the early 2000s; a limited re-release in 2019.[^21][^25]

items.name: Coca-Cola Classic
items.text: The old formula, back from July 1985 and the leading brand in 1990.[^6][^14] The word “Classic” came off US labels from 2009.[^19]

items.name: Pepsi
items.text: At 18.8% before the change.[^6] It said May 1985 was its best month ever, and ended the decade behind Classic.[^5][^14]

items.name: Diet Coke
items.text: The project that produced the new formula, officials said.[^6] Third among all brands in 1990.[^14]

blocks.source: UPI, Jun 10 and Jul 10, 1985[^5][^6]; UPI, Jan 25, 1991, citing Beverage Industry magazine[^14]; Snopes[^16]; the Associated Press[^19]. Figures from different publishers are not strictly comparable.

blocks.title: What Pepsi said
blocks.body: On the day of the reversal a Pepsi spokesman told UPI: “We’re not surprised to hear Coke is reintroducing its old formula because quite clearly the new formula was universally hated.”[^6] Beverage Digest’s publisher, Jesse Meyers, saw something else in the same decision: a market “getting incredibly diversified,” in which Coca-Cola had found a way “to add another segment.”[^6]
